presenceLabel: Wyandot town, raid or hunting area here
presenceNote: Wyandot towns were north of the Ohio (Michilimackinac from 1671, Detroit from 1701, Sandusky Bay, the Muskingum and the Sandusky River). The nation is shown 1671–1843 (medium confidence for the named sites, low–medium for the county tint). The Kentucky link is raids (1780, 1782) and hunting or travel on the Warriors Path; no Wyandot camp in Kentucky is documented. The Kentucky raid story is shown for 1780–1782. The place-name story has no dates. The tint shows a general area drawn from whole counties, not a boundary.
overlapNote: Shared Ohio country with Delaware (Fort McIntosh 1785 gave the land to both), Shawnee (Wyandot claimed the Shawnee lands west of the Miami in the 1789 Fort Harmar record: 'the Shawanese are only living upon it by their permission'), Mingo and Odawa. In Kentucky the same hunting grounds were used by Shawnee, Delaware, Mingo, Miami (Henderson 1992) and claimed by Shawnee, Cherokee and, by sale, Six Nations.
basis: Treaty text (Fort McIntosh 1785, Greenville 1795), Wyandotte Nation history page, Wikipedia for the 1780/1782 raids, USFS appendix for the name. Town points from Wikipedia coordinates.

wyandot-name-kah-ten-tah-teh-fair-land-o.presenceNote: This story is about a place name, not a territory: it has no dates and no mapped boundary. The Wyandot themselves lived north of the Ohio (Sandusky River, Detroit); their link to Kentucky was hunting and travel on the Warriors Path, and raids in 1780 and 1782 (see the Wyandot raids story).

eras.label: 1671–1700 · Michilimackinac
eras.text: After the Iroquois dispersed the Petun and Wendat in 1649, the refugees moved between Mackinac Island, Wisconsin and Lake Superior and in 1671 settled at Michilimackinac, where the Jesuits had a mission at St. Ignace (Wikipedia). The tint is Mackinac County, Michigan, a whole county, approximate; the earlier stops are not drawn.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · named site approximate

eras.label: 1701–1737 · Detroit
eras.text: In 1701 Cadillac invited the Wendat at Michilimackinac to settle near Fort Pontchartrain at Detroit (Wikipedia). They were then effectively the Wyandot. The tint is Wayne County, Michigan, a whole county, and the point is approximate.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · named site approximate

eras.label: 1738–1762 · Sandusky Bay, Conchake and Detroit
eras.text: In 1738 the Wendat moved to Sandusky Bay, and after returning to Detroit in 1739 split in two. Orontony’s faction founded Junundat south of Sandusky Bay. After a failed attack on Fort Detroit in 1747 it moved to Conchake at the head of the Muskingum River (1747 to about 1752), then returned to Sandusky Bay; Junundat was destroyed in 1763 (Wikipedia). The tint is Detroit, Sandusky Bay and Coshocton County as whole counties, approximate, not a boundary.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · named sites approximate

eras.label: c.1763–1779 · Sandusky River and Detroit towns
eras.text: After Junundat was destroyed in 1763 the Sandusky Wyandot moved west to the Sandusky River valley (Upper Sandusky), while others stayed at Detroit (Wikipedia). Their towns were north of the Ohio. The tint is a general area built from whole counties (the Sandusky River country and the Detroit area): approximate, not a boundary. Detroit and Sandusky points are approximate.

eras.label: 1780–1782 · Raids on Kentucky stations
eras.text: Wyandot warriors took part in the June 1780 attacks on Ruddle's and Martin's Stations, then in the 15-17 Aug 1782 siege of Bryan Station beside Lenape, Shawnee and Caldwell's Rangers, and in the ambush at Blue Licks on 19 Aug. They came from their towns on the Sandusky River and near Detroit (the tinted general area, approximate). The Kentucky points mark events, not Wyandot camps. No Kentucky camp site is documented.

eras.label: 1785 · Fort McIntosh allotment
eras.text: The 21 Jan 1785 Fort McIntosh treaty allotted the lands inside its line to the Wyandot and Delaware “to live and to hunt on”, with Ottawa already living there, and made them give up land east, south and west: about one third of Ohio. The hatched counties are an approximation north of the legs of the line the treaty text lets us place; the west and south closure is ambiguous in the text. Approximate, not a boundary.
eras.apprTag: Approximate area · county approximation of the allotment

eras.label: 1795–1816 · Greenville
eras.text: At Greenville (3 Aug 1795) the Wyandot, with Delaware, Shawnee, Miami and others, ceded land east and south of the Greenville line (hatched, simplified; the line ends on the Ohio opposite the mouth of the Kentucky River). The tinted general area of the Wyandot towns lay north and west of that line.

eras.label: 1817–1843 · Fort Meigs reserves and removal
eras.text: The 1817 Treaty of Fort Meigs gave the Wyandot a tract twelve miles square at Upper Sandusky, centred on Fort Ferree, and a one-mile square at the cranberry swamp on Broken Sword Creek (treaty text, Wyandotte archive). The Brownstown reserve near Detroit was ceded in 1818. Most Wyandot were removed from Ohio to Kansas in the early 1840s, leaving in 1843 (Wikipedia). The tint is Wyandot and Crawford counties, Ohio, with Wayne County, Michigan, as whole counties; it is not a reserve boundary.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · named site approximate

eras.label: Undated · Kah-ten-tah-teh (place name)
eras.text: The U.S. Forest Service history appendix records that Wyandots who often came south of the Ohio to hunt or to travel the Warriors Path called the country Kah-ten-tah-teh, “Fair Land of Tomorrow”. A name is not a territory: this page has no boundary and no dates, and nothing is drawn on the map.

Wyandot towns on the Sandusky River (Upper Sandusky, Wyandot and Sandusky counties) and near Detroit (Wayne and Monroe counties, Michigan), widened to the neighbouring Ohio counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Ohio counties north of the sourced legs of the Fort McIntosh line (Cuyahoga mouth, Tuscarawas portage, Fort Laurens, Pickawillany); the treaty text leaves the west and south closure ambiguous. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
Land east and south of the Greenville line in Ohio and Indiana (same simplified polygon as the Shawnee page).
Mackinac County, Michigan, where St. Ignace and Michilimackinac lie, as a whole county. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
Wayne County, Michigan (Detroit), as a whole county. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Detroit (Wayne County), Sandusky Bay (Sandusky and Erie counties, Ohio, around Junundat) and Conchake at the head of the Muskingum (Coshocton County, Ohio), as whole counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Upper Sandusky (Wyandot County) and the cranberry-swamp tract on Broken Sword Creek (Crawford County), Ohio, from the 1817 treaty, plus Wayne County, Michigan (Detroit). Whole counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
St. Ignace, Michigan (Wikipedia 45.874, -84.726), site of the Jesuit mission at the Straits of Mackinac where the Wendat and Petun settled in 1671 (Wikipedia). Approximate.
